Interpreting local LLM throughput measurements requires understanding the context in which those numbers are generated, as well as the limitations of the metrics themselves. Throughput, typically measured in tokens per second (TPS) or prompts per second (PPS), is a useful proxy for performance, but it must be interpreted with caution. The key metrics to consider are prompt throughput (how many prompts the model can process per second) and generation throughput (how many tokens the model can generate per second). These metrics are often reported separately because they reflect different stages of the inference pipeline and may be constrained by different bottlenecks.

Prompt throughput measures how quickly the model can process a batch of input prompts — this includes tokenization, model forward passes, and output decoding. It’s often the most relevant metric for applications that require rapid response to user queries, such as chatbots or search interfaces. However, prompt throughput can be artificially inflated if the prompts are very short — for example, a 10-token prompt may be processed faster than a 100-token prompt, even if the model’s internal computation is more complex. This is because the model’s computational load scales with input length, but the overhead of setting up the computation (e.g., memory allocation, kernel launches) remains relatively constant. Therefore, prompt throughput is most meaningful when comparing models or hardware configurations using prompts of similar length and complexity.

Generation throughput, on the other hand, measures how many tokens the model can generate per second. This is often more indicative of the model’s true computational efficiency, especially for long-form generation tasks. However, generation throughput can be misleading if the output is very short — for instance, a model generating a 10-token response may report a high TPS, but this doesn’t reflect its ability to handle longer sequences. In such cases, the model may be spending most of its time on the initial prompt processing, and the generation phase is trivial. To get a more accurate picture, it’s best to measure generation throughput using prompts that require substantial output — such as 100–500 tokens — and to average across multiple runs to smooth out variance.

When comparing CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs, it’s important to recognize that each configuration has different performance characteristics. CPU-only runs are typically slower but more energy-efficient and more portable — they’re useful for edge devices or systems with limited GPU resources. GPU-only runs, especially with modern architectures like NVIDIA’s Ada Lovelace or AMD’s RDNA 3, can achieve much higher throughput due to parallel processing and optimized tensor cores. Hybrid runs — which use both CPU and GPU — can be more complex to benchmark because they involve data transfer overhead and load balancing. In hybrid setups, throughput may be limited by the speed of data movement between CPU and GPU memory, or by the CPU’s ability to keep the GPU busy. Therefore, when comparing configurations, it’s essential to use the same prompt length, batch size, and model parameters — and to measure both prompt and generation throughput to get a complete picture.

Another critical consideration is the batch size. Throughput scales with batch size — larger batches can saturate the model’s parallelism, but they also increase memory usage and may introduce latency due to memory bandwidth bottlenecks. Therefore, throughput measurements should always be reported alongside the batch size used. Additionally, it’s important to use consistent hardware and software environments — for example, different CUDA versions or driver versions can affect performance — so that comparisons are fair.

In summary, interpreting local LLM throughput requires understanding the context of the measurement, the nature of the prompts, and the hardware configuration. Prompt throughput is useful for fast-response applications, but generation throughput is more indicative of true model efficiency. Very short outputs can mislead because they don’t reflect the model
